questions.qtext:
Consider the following two graphs $G$ (on left), $H$(on right):


Which of the following statements is/are true for $G$, $H$ ?

options.text: The above two graphs have the same number of vertices.
The above two graphs have the same number of edges.
The above two graphs have the same degree sequences.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

What does it mean for two graphs to be isomorphic?

Ans: Put simply, these two graphs have the same structure.

More formally, two graphs, $G$ and $H$, are isomorphic if there exists a bijection between $V(G)$ and $V(H), f: V(G) \longrightarrow V(H)$, where $u v \in E(G)$ if and only if $f(u) f(v) \in E(H)$. Isomorphism is denoted: $G \cong H$.

If $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ are isomorphic graphs then they have the same number of vertices, the same number of edges, and the same degree sequence. BUT the converse is Not true.


The converse is: "If two graphs $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ have the same number of vertices, same number of edges, and the same degree sequence, then they are isomorphic". This statement is false.


The above two graphs have the same number of vertices, edges and identical degree sequences, but are not isomorphic since the leftmost graph has no five cycles, while the rightmost graph has two.
